Sarah developed a strong foundation in signal processing, communications systems, and real-time computing. Coursework included Digital Signal Processing (Python), Communication Systems, Electronic System Design, Control Systems, and Simulation of Engineering Systems.

Her final year project focused on real-time EEG signal processing, investigating signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) limits in brain-computer interface tasks. She developed software in Python and C++ for filtering, feature extraction, and real-time analysis of noisy biological signals.
This work provided a strong mathematical and programming foundation that later supported advanced study in Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence.
Program Overview: Electronics with Music BEng (Hons)

The Electronics with Music BEng (Hons) at the University of Glasgow combines the world of music with a thorough study of modern electronics. This unique fusion of arts and engineering produces graduates who are fully qualified electronics engineers with particular skills in music technology.

Glasgow is a UNESCO City of Music, providing an exceptional environment where students can study performance, composition, and technology alongside a range of other music options. The program is approximately two-thirds engineering-based, with the remaining third dedicated to music studies,
the remaining third dedicated to music studies, ensuring students develop strong technical foundations alongside creative expertise.

Teaching is delivered through a combination of lectures, small group tutorials, and seminars. Students gain practical experience in music technology laboratories, the recording studio, electronic design laboratories, and with a range of modern computing systems.

Programme structure

Students study the same courses in the first three years whether they are on the BEng or MEng degree programme. Approximately two-thirds of these programmes are engineering based.
Year 1

Students take courses in mathematics and key engineering fundamentals including computing and analogue & digital electronics. These courses are supported by individual and group project and laboratory work.

The music component includes the courses Listening in culture and Listening through analysis. The first encourages an open-minded, multidisciplinary approach to listening and writing about music of all genres and styles, while the second explores more analytical and musicological approaches to the
analytical and musicological approaches to the understanding and analysis of musical works and events, as experienced through notation, live performance, recording or audiovisual media.
Years 2 and 3
Year 2 involves core engineering subjects of analogue & digital electronics, electrical circuits and computer systems. These courses are reinforced by a design project and mathematics.

Students also take two courses of their choice in music. Choices include the Sonic arts foundation course, focusing on creative recording and manipulation of sound, Critical listening and Building and using interactive computer-based tools; as well as a range of other courses including Composition,
a range of other courses including Composition, Jazz, Aesthetics & philosophy of music and Music analysis.

The third year delves deeper into such engineering topics as systems design, communication systems, control, real-time systems, electromagnetic compatibility and mathematics. Most courses are supported by laboratory and project work. As part of the music component, students can take further Sonic

music component, students can take further Sonic arts courses focusing on sound for narrative film and interactive audiovisual media; or other music options of their choice, including Composition, Performance, Jazz, Aesthetics & philosophy of music and a range of historical topics.
Year 4

In year 4, students also take two courses in music, alongside their engineering options. They might continue their study of Sonic Arts, taking an individual creative project; or take further options in music, including Composition, Performance, Jazz, Aesthetics & philosophy of music or historical
Aesthetics & philosophy of music or historical topics.

Artificial Intelligence MSc

Part of: AI, Computer and Data Science

This MSc allows students to deepen their understanding of AI from the principles behind intelligent systems to the technologies pushing the field forward. Students specialise in the areas that interest them most and broaden their understanding of machine learning, natural language processing, and

learning, natural language processing, and the ethical questions surrounding AI. They gain hands-on experience with technologies including deep neural networks and large language models. Students work with relevant tools through exercises and lab sessions and graduate with the practical AI skills
and graduate with the practical AI skills needed for careers in machine learning, data engineering, software engineering and AI research.

Students can choose between two specialist streams: Language and Agents or Multimodal AI.
    Students gain experience with cutting-edge tools such as Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL) and Large Language Models (LLM).

Students complete an individual project, with past topics including music recommendation using global-context embeddings, automated damage inspection with deep learning and deception detection using machine learning.

The degree is recognised towards Chartered IT (CITP) Professional and Chartered Engineer (CEng) registration.
What students study

This MSc allows students to focus their studies and combine different AI topics to suit their personal requirements and future plans. The programme combines world-class teaching, research, and industrial connections to help students understand fundamental AI concepts. Students study universal
fundamental AI concepts. Students study universal machine learning tools essential for any AI job profile, as well as practical and research skills across various AI topics.

Students gain experience with cutting-edge tools such as Deep Neural Networks (DNN), Deep Reinforcement Learning (Deep RL), and Large Language Models (LLMs) through regular exercises and practical labs. They work closely with lecturers and supervisors to carry out a major project on the AI topic
to carry out a major project on the AI topic they wish to specialise in.
The MSc Artificial Intelligence (AI) is structured in two different streams.

All students study a set of compulsory modules covering the fundamentals of machine learning, artificial intelligence, natural language processing, and ethics, regulation, and law in digital information processing and decision making.

In addition to the compulsory modules, students choose one educational stream of elective modules during Welcome Week, based on their interests.
Professional Recognition

This degree is accredited by BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, for the purposes of partially meeting the academic requirement for registration as a Chartered IT Professional. It is also accredited by BCS, The Chartered Institute for IT, on behalf of the Engineering Council, for the purposes of
of the Engineering Council, for the purposes of partially meeting the academic requirement for registration as a Chartered Engineer.

In addition, this degree is accredited by the Institution of Engineering and Technology on behalf of the Engineering Council as meeting the requirements for Further Learning for registration as a Chartered Engineer. Candidates must hold a CEng accredited BEng/BSc (Hons) undergraduate first degree
BEng/BSc (Hons) undergraduate first degree to comply with full CEng registration requirements.

Language learning has always been an interest of Sarah's. As a child, she loved secret codes and ciphers and working out how to decode them. Later, at school, she studied French and Latin.
French was particularly useful because Sarah visited France several times as a child and loved being able to decipher the signs and conversations around her.

However, Latin was a subject she particularly loved, so much so that she studied it for A-level. Anyone familiar with Latin will know that it has a particularly complex grammar structure, which Sarah saw as a challenge. Unlike modern languages, where learning to speak is a significant element,

where learning to speak is a significant element, Latin teaching focuses more on translating text and literature, which appealed to her love of decoding. It also introduced her to some classical texts in their original language and to some interesting classical history that she might otherwise not
classical history that she might otherwise not have been exposed to.

Continuing her study of romance languages, Sarah went on to study Italian as an extracurricular activity outside school because she had Italian family friends, and more recently she decided to learn more about languages with different grammar structures. She is currently trying to teach herself
She is currently trying to teach herself some Norwegian, which has a more similar grammatical structure to English and has therefore been exciting to explore.

Music has always been a big part of Sarah's life. She started learning the piano when she was six years old and later picked up the violin. It turns out the piano is not one of her natural gifts, but she has continued playing the violin.

Sarah is currently working toward her Grade 8 violin exam, which is a long-term goal of hers. This is very exciting for her because she is now studying some very well-known pieces of music, such as Vivaldi's 'Spring', which she has always wanted to learn to play.

Sarah finds music to be a very rewarding hobby and enjoys the process of learning new pieces and improving her skills. She also finds that both listening to and playing music is a great way to relax and unwind after a long day.

When Sarah was younger, her father used to travel to many different places for work, which perhaps inspired her interest in travelling. Her father encouraged her interest in different places by taking her on trips when she was young, and she has continued to enjoy travelling as an adult.

Since she has been old enough to book her own trips, Sarah has enjoyed planning itineraries for both weekend city breaks in Europe and longer trips. There are so many different places in the world, with so many different cultures, landscapes, and animals, and she hopes to be lucky enough to travel

and she hopes to be lucky enough to travel widely. She thinks it is important to experience different cultures and ways of life, and she finds travelling to be a great way to broaden her horizons and learn about the world around her.
